summary: Bitcoin is a peer-to-peer electronic cash system that enables online payments without a trusted third party by using a distributed timestamp server and proof-of-work to prevent double-spending. The network timestamps transactions by hashing them into a chain of proof-of-work, and security relies on honest nodes controlling a majority of CPU power.

claims.text: Bitcoin is a purely peer-to-peer version of electronic cash that allows online payments to be sent directly from one party to another without going through a financial institution.
claims.evidence_quote: A purely peer-to-peer version of electronic cash would allow online payments to be sent directly from one party to another without going through a financial institution.

claims.text: The network timestamps transactions by hashing them into an ongoing chain of hash-based proof-of-work, forming a record that cannot be changed without redoing the proof-of-work.
claims.evidence_quote: The network timestamps transactions by hashing them into an ongoing chain of hash-based proof-of-work, forming a record that cannot be changed without redoing the proof-of-work.

claims.text: The system is secure as long as honest nodes collectively control more CPU power than any cooperating group of attacker nodes.
claims.evidence_quote: The system is secure as long as honest nodes collectively control more CPU power than any cooperating group of attacker nodes.

claims.text: A timestamp server works by taking a hash of a block of items to be timestamped and widely publishing the hash, such as in a newspaper or Usenet post.
claims.evidence_quote: A timestamp server works by taking a hash of a block of items to be timestamped and widely publishing the hash, such as in a newspaper or Usenet post.

claims.text: The proof-of-work involves scanning for a value that when hashed, such as with SHA-256, the hash begins with a number of zero bits.
claims.evidence_quote: The proof-of-work involves scanning for a value that when hashed, such as with SHA-256, the hash begins with a number of zero bits.

claims.text: The first transaction in a block is a special transaction that starts a new coin owned by the creator of the block, providing an incentive for nodes to support the network.
claims.evidence_quote: By convention, the first transaction in a block is a special transaction that starts a new coin owned by the creator of the block.

claims.text: Once a predetermined number of coins have entered circulation, the incentive can transition entirely to transaction fees and be completely inflation free.
claims.evidence_quote: Once a predetermined number of coins have entered circulation, the incentive can transition entirely to transaction fees and be completely inflation free.

claims.text: A block header with no transactions would be about 80 bytes, and with blocks generated every 10 minutes, that amounts to 4.2MB per year.
claims.evidence_quote: A block header with no transactions would be about 80 bytes. If we suppose blocks are generated every 10 minutes, 80 bytes * 6 * 24 * 365 = 4.2MB per year.

claims.text: Simplified payment verification allows a user to verify payments without running a full network node by keeping a copy of the block headers of the longest proof-of-work chain.
claims.evidence_quote: It is possible to verify payments without running a full network node. A user only needs to keep a copy of the block headers of the longest proof-of-work chain.

claims.text: Privacy can be maintained by keeping public keys anonymous, and a new key pair should be used for each transaction to keep them from being linked to a common owner.
claims.evidence_quote: privacy can still be maintained by breaking the flow of information in another place: by keeping public keys anonymous.

claims.text: The probability of an attacker catching up from a given deficit is analogous to a Gambler's Ruin problem, and it drops exponentially as the number of blocks the attacker has to catch up with increases.
claims.evidence_quote: The probability of an attacker catching up from a given deficit is analogous to a Gambler's Ruin problem.

claims.text: For an attacker with 10% of the network (q=0.1), the probability of catching up from 5 blocks behind is 0.0009137.
To keep the probability of an attacker catching up below 0.1%, if the attacker has 10% of the network, the recipient should wait for 5 confirmations; if 30%, wait for 24 confirmations.
